prompt: Which are the four parts of a structured interview, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Questions, sameness, a scale, and an order.

choices.text: Each interviewer scores alone before discussing
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Every candidate gets the same questions
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Answers are scored against an anchored scale
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The candidate chooses which questions to answer
choices.why: No: that would make candidates incomparable.

choices.text: Questions come from the job
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: Why does each of Caju’s four interviewers own one area instead of asking a bit of everything?

choices.text: Four deep interviews produce four pieces of evidence; four shallow ones, overlapping impressions
choices.why: Right: depth on one must gives evidence that the others do not duplicate.

choices.text: To save time
choices.why: The total time is the same; what changes is what it produces.

choices.text: Because interviewers are only qualified in one area
choices.why: Qualification is part of who gets which area, not the reason for splitting them.

choices.text: So candidates do not get bored
choices.why: Not the reason given.

prompt: When does the lesson say situational questions work better than behavioural ones?
hint: Who may not have a past example?

choices.text: For senior candidates, who have so many past examples that choosing one becomes a distraction
choices.why: Senior candidates are usually the ones with good past examples to draw on.

choices.text: Always
choices.why: Behavioural questions are the premise of the method; situational ones are for a particular case.

choices.text: When no scale has been written
choices.why: Situational questions need a scale more, not less.

choices.text: For less experienced candidates
choices.why: Right: they may not have a past example, though the answers need a scale even more.

prompt: Why does Helena, the product manager, interview on the trade-off conversation?

choices.text: Product managers must be on every panel
choices.why: No such rule is given.

choices.text: To balance the panel with somebody who is not an engineer, which candidates find reassuring
choices.why: Balance may be a side effect; the reason given is that she receives the explanations.

choices.text: She will be on the receiving end of them
choices.why: Right: the person the must serves is well placed to assess it.

choices.text: Because Renata was busy
choices.why: Renata runs the fourth conversation.

prompt: What does a validity of 0 mean for a hiring method?

choices.text: It predicts nothing
choices.why: Right: 1 would be perfect; the best methods sit between about 0.3 and 0.5.

choices.text: It predicts perfectly
choices.why: That would be 1.

choices.text: It is illegal
choices.why: Validity is a statistical measure, not a legal status.

choices.text: It has never been studied by anybody, so nothing at all is known about how well it works
choices.why: A measured validity of 0 is a finding, not an absence of study.

prompt: Match each estimate with its source.
An experienced interviewer says they can tell within five minutes whether a candidate is good. What does the lesson say about that?
hint: What does research on unstructured interviews measure?

choices.text: Experience makes intuition reliable
choices.why: The research does not find that.

choices.text: Research on unstructured interviews measures that intuition, and it comes out well below structure
choices.why: Right: the confidence is common and the evidence does not support it.

choices.text: Five minutes is enough for most roles
choices.why: Not a claim the lesson makes.

choices.text: It is true for senior interviewers
choices.why: Renata’s own reaction, that the research applied to others, is the trap.

prompt: A structured interview has a validity of about 0.42. What follows, by the lesson?

choices.text: Many who interview well will not perform well, so the decision needs humility
choices.why: Right: the best method is still noisy.

choices.text: It predicts 42% of hires correctly
choices.why: A correlation is not a hit rate.

choices.text: It is worse than an unstructured interview
choices.why: Unstructured came out at about 0.19 in the same review.

choices.text: It guarantees that the company’s own interview works as well as the average in the research
choices.why: The figures are averages; a particular interview works only if it reflects the job.

prompt: What did Laszlo Bock say Google had found about brainteasers?

choices.text: A complete waste of time
choices.why: Right: and that their main function was to make the interviewer feel smart.

choices.text: The best predictor of engineering skill
choices.why: The opposite of what he said.

choices.text: Useful only for senior roles
choices.why: Not what he said.

choices.text: Good for measuring how candidates think under pressure, which every engineering job involves
choices.why: Pressure at a puzzle is not what the job asks for, which is the lesson’s point.

prompt: At the coffee machine, an interviewer asks a candidate, “Do you have kids?” What does the lesson say?
hint: If it would not be on the sheet…

choices.text: It must not be asked, coffee or not
choices.why: Right: the candidate may reasonably think it was part of the interview, and it is a discriminatory question.

choices.text: It is small talk and does not count
choices.why: Small talk is exactly where these questions slip in.

choices.text: It is fine if asked of every candidate equally
choices.why: Asking everybody does not make it relevant or lawful.

choices.text: It is useful context for whether the person will be able to cover on-call weeks and holidays
choices.why: That is exactly the kind of inference the law forbids basing a decision on.

prompt: Why does “What is your greatest weakness?” tell an interviewer little?

choices.text: A rehearsed strength
choices.why: Right: candidates prepare it, and it measures preparation rather than the must list.

choices.text: It is illegal in Brazil
choices.why: It is not illegal; it is uninformative.

choices.text: Candidates refuse to answer it
choices.why: They answer it readily, with something prepared.

choices.text: Because weaknesses do not matter for engineering roles as long as the code works
choices.why: Weaknesses matter; this question does not reveal them.

prompt: Put the levels of Helena’s scale in order, from 1 to 4.
items: No real example, or technical terms
A real example, still technical, unchecked
Clear, in the listener’s terms, trade-off as outcomes
Adapted when not followed, knows what was decided

prompt: What makes Helena’s scale usable by two different interviewers?

choices.text: It has four levels instead of ten
choices.why: The number of levels matters less than what each describes.

choices.text: Helena trains every interviewer on it personally before each round
choices.why: A briefing helps, but the descriptions are what make it shared.

choices.text: Each level describes what is in the answer, and levels differ by observable steps
choices.why: Right: so two people hearing the same answer land on the same number, or one apart.

choices.text: It uses adjectives like “strong” and “weak”
choices.why: Adjectives are what an anchored scale replaces.

prompt: Halfway through the round, Helena notices many candidates misunderstand her question. What is her rule?
hint: Same test for everybody in a round.

choices.text: Rewrite it before the next candidate
choices.why: That breaks the sameness the structure depends on.

choices.text: Drop the question from the round entirely and score the remaining three conversations only
choices.why: Dropping it loses the must it assesses.

choices.text: For the next role
choices.why: Right: changing it now would give later candidates a different test.

choices.text: Give everybody a 3
choices.why: That would make the scores meaningless.

prompt: An interviewer’s note says: “4. Great communicator, really impressive, would love to work with her.” What is wrong with it?

choices.text: A 4 is never justified
choices.why: A 4 is fine when the answer meets the level’s description.

choices.text: It is too short
choices.why: Short is fine; Helena’s note is two lines. The problem is what it contains.

choices.text: It records impressions instead of what she said, so nobody is able to check the 4 against the scale
choices.why: Right: the evidence should be close to the candidate’s words, mapped to the level’s description.

choices.text: It should have been written after the debrief, once the others had shared their views
choices.why: Scoring before the debrief is one of the four parts of structure.
